theme: David mourns Saul; anointed over Judah; Ish-bosheth
readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 1:1-3:39. David grieves for Saul and Jonathan, and becomes king, first over Judah and then over a divided kingdom. Read his lament in chapter 1 carefully.
settingTheScene: The second book of Samuel opens with a messenger bringing news of Saul’s death. David’s response is grief, not triumph. After the lament, God directs David to Hebron, where he is anointed king over Judah. For seven and a half years, there is civil war between David’s house and the house of Saul. Abner, Saul’s commander, eventually switches sides, and is murdered by Joab.
observation: A man claims to have killed Saul and brings his crown to David. David has him executed because he “stretched out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed” (1:14-16).
David’s lament: “How the mighty have fallen!” (1:19, 25, 27).
“Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In life and in death they were not divided” (1:23).
“I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women” (1:26).
David inquires of the LORD, goes up to Hebron, and is anointed king over Judah (2:1-4).
“There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger” (3:1).
Abner makes a covenant with David, and Joab kills Abner in revenge for his brother (3:12-27).
David mourns Abner and says, “Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?” (3:31-38).
interpretation:
David’s first act as the next king is to weep. The man who brings Saul’s crown expects a reward, but David has him killed. David has consistently honored Saul as the LORD’s anointed, and he will not profit from his death, even by a messenger’s lie. There is no gloating in his heart.

The lament in chapter 1 is a work of poetry and of real love. David praises Saul, who had pursued him for years, and Jonathan, his friend. He does not mention Saul’s failures. He mourns a king who fell, and he honors the good. The refrain “How the mighty have fallen!” echoes through the poem like a bell. It teaches that grief for the fallen is compatible with God’s judgment, and that we should be slow to speak ill of the dead.

When David is anointed in Hebron, he is told to go there by the LORD. He inquires. He has learned the lesson of dependence. But notice that he does not rush to take the whole kingdom. The war between the houses lasts seven years. He waits, and “David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker.”

The story of Abner and Joab shows the dangers of power. Abner brings the northern tribes over to David, a great peace. But Joab, for personal revenge, murders Abner. It is a stain on David’s reign. David declares his innocence, curses Joab’s house, and mourns publicly. He composes another lament for Abner. The people are pleased, “for all the people took note of it.” Yet David admits, “I am this day weak, though anointed king” (3:39). He is aware of the limits of his power.

The chapters teach that God’s promise is fulfilled slowly. David is king, but he must still grieve, wait, and deal with violence in his own camp.
connection: Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35). He too was anointed king and had to wait for his kingdom. Hebrews 2:8-9 says, “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him… crowned with glory and honor.” Paul says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).
application:
Think of someone who has hurt you and has since died or fallen. Can you honor what was good in them?

Wait on God for what he has promised. Do not force the timing.

Grieve honestly over the losses in your life, and bring them to him.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to grieve well and honor the fallen.
Ask him to make you patient as you wait for his promises.
Thank Jesus, the King who wept and will reign.
